newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Bahrain Emir vows to defend island's integrity.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain Emir vows to defend island's integrity.

text.p: Bahrain on Monday marked its silver jubilee with a pledge from the Emir to defend the Gulf state's integrity by all means.
Sheikh Isa bin Sulman al-Khalifa vowed not to compromise on any part of the island, which is locked with neighbouring Qatar in a bitter territorial dispute.
"No part of the entity of this homeland shall be squandered or compromised," he said in a speech on Bahraini television.
A dispute over a cluster of reefs, sandbanks and islands controlled by Bahrain since the 1930s but claimed by Qatar has led to increased tension with its neighbour in recent weeks.
Bahrain, a British protectorate from 1861 to 1971, has been the scene of sporadic internal unrest in which about 27 people have died over the last two years.

Dissident members of its majority Shi'ite Moslem community seek economic and political reforms by the country's Sunni rulers including restoration of parliament dissolved in 1975 and lifting of a ban on political parties.

Sheikh Isa made no specific mention of waves of protests, violence and arson attacks since December 1994. On Sunday he decreed the release of scores of prisoners including some held in connection with anti-government unrest.

"On the basis of the ability of this nation to adhere to its rights and principles, and to face covetous ambitions from any source, Bahrain will pursue the defence of the unity of its national soil and its territorial integrity by all legitimate means," the emir said.
"The source of our confidence stems from the ability of this country, government and people, to surmount various difficulties encountered in the past and still being encountered."
Sheikh Isa said the economy of Bahrain, the first Gulf Arab state to discover oil in commercial quantities in 1932, was witnessing positive and encouraging trends.
"This indicates progress in the performance of our national economy, despite difficult economic conditions the region and the world are experiencing."

He said this would pave the way for the government to implement several housing, educational and health projects as well as others which promoted the infrastructure and contributed towards providing better services.
Bahrain is the smallest and least wealthy of the Gulf oil states with production which has dwindled since the 1970s to 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) from its own oilfields.
In April Saudi Arabia, with which Bahrain is linked by a 25 km (16 miles) causeway, donated the entire 140,000 bpd output from an offshore field they shared.
Bahrain Monetary Agency (BMA), the central bank, said in its annual report oil revenues in 1995 rose 11.8 percent to 318.6 million dinars ($845.0 million) from 285.1 million in 1994.
The increase helped Bahrain's trade balance to record a surplus of 157.1 million dinars in 1995, the first since 1991, compared with a deficit of 49.3 million dinars in 1994, it said.
Bahrain has diversified its economy by creating small industries to benefit from gas reserves.

It is the Middle East's largest aluminium producer with annual capacity of 460,000 tonnes and has developed into the main banking and financial centre in the Gulf with 48 Offshore Banking Units and many commercial banks, representative offices, foreign exchange brokers and investment advisers.
